title: ‘Super tax’ puts SMSFs on red alert
full_text:
Jim Chalmers could be forced into another backdown on part of his tax reform package after the self-managed super fund industry’s peak body warned hundreds of thousands of superannuants would face higher effective tax rates because of the new rules on capital gains.
On Tuesday, the Financial Services Council identified that Labor’s new rules on how losses can be offset against gains within certain investment vehicles used by super funds would effectively increase the tax burden of millions of retirees. A super fund that invests through a managed investment trust will now pay more tax than a fund that holds the same asset directly instead of through a trust.
While one of the biggest super funds in the country urged the Treasurer to rethink the new rules in the same way he reconsidered the so-called widows’ tax and death tax also born out of the May budget, the peak body for self-managed super funds joined in demanding he reverse course.
“There are hundreds of thousands of SMSFs that have investments in vehicles such as managed investment schemes so we are concerned they will all be subject to the new capital loss ordering rules and therefore those SMSFs could end up paying higher effective tax rates on their investments,” SMSF Association chief executive Peter Burgess said.
“We agree with the FSC that this is a significant issue that needs to be addressed. According to the most recent ATO stats, SMSFs have $264bn across listed, unlisted and ‘other managed investments’ which potentially will be impacted.” David Travers, chief executive of the Australian Custodial Services Association, which is responsible for holding members accountable for monitoring Australians’ superannuation wealth, said he did not know whether Dr Chalmers would reverse his decision. “We have asked Treasury for clarification. We are waiting for a response,” he said.
Treasury said consultation over the changes applied to such trusts finished last week.
The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia said it would make a submission about this issue and it had been granted an extension by Treasury.
The new capital loss ordering rules mean that MITs cannot apply capital losses first against capital gains that are not eligible for the CGT discount before applying any remaining losses against discount-eligible gains.
CPA Australia’s head of tax policy Jenny Wong said the uncertainty about whether this would be enforced was a reflection of poor tax reform planning.
“Problems keep surfacing in this package because of how it was put together,” she said.
“Consultation on the exposure draft ran for a little over a fortnight in August, even though the original proposal was for no consultation at all. That isn’t enough time for Treasury to stress-test the interactions, let alone for the professions to do it for them,” she said.
“The loss ordering issue raised this week is a textbook example of the kind of problem a proper consultation timetable exists to catch.” “Whether or not the outcome was intended, two people with the same underlying investment end up in different positions based purely on the structure they happen to be invested through.” “That is a design flaw, and it should be fixed before the bill is introduced, not after.” The Coalition leapt on the revelations of a stealth tax on super. “The Albanese government has been caught laying yet another tax landmine in its budget to feed its spending addiction, and this time it’s targeting superannuation” said Treasury spokesman Tim Wilson.
Assistant Treasury and financial services spokesman Kevin Hogan said: “Labor’s first super tax was aimed at high balances. This one is different.
“It hits anyone whose super is invested indirectly – for example, through an exchange traded fund (ETF), managed fund, or property trust. Millions of Australians’ retirements will be impacted. “Capital gains inside super are meant to be taxed at an effective 10 per cent. Under Labor’s new tax, some of those gains will now be taxed at 15 per cent.”
